cover.title: DittoFS, from the outside in
cover.lead: DittoFS is a file server for NFS and SMB clients that keeps its files in a bucket. This introduction shows who uses it, what runs inside it, and how one write travels from a client to the bucket.
cover.built: Built from DittoFS's design documents and code overview, at commit bc7aa99
cover.notes: The one deck not tied to a single RFC. Sources: docs/internals/rfcs/rfc-0-data-lifecycle.md ('Start here', Glossary, §1 Scope, §4.2, §5, §10) for the design, docs/internals/architecture.md for today's code, and README.md for what DittoFS is. Commit bc7aa99. The RFCs specify the target design; one slide near the end compares today's code with the design. Keys: → next, S speaker notes, ? help. Click any underlined term for its definition. The badge's sources: RFC 0 and docs/internals/architecture.md at bc7aa99.

learn.title: What you'll learn
items: Who uses DittoFS, and what they see when they mount a [[share]].
The parts inside one [[node]], and how a request crosses them.
One write, followed from the client to the bucket and back.
What survives a crash, and how NFS and SMB share one file.
Where today's code differs from the design, and which section to read next.
learn.notes: The deck's own framing. Every later section of the home page has its own deck; this one introduces them and ends with a map of them.

what.title: What DittoFS is
what.lead: DittoFS is a file server that runs as an ordinary program. Clients mount it as they would a NAS box, and their files end up in a cheap object store.
what.c1: Linux and macOS mount it over NFS and Windows over SMB, and all of them reach the same [[share|shares]] at the same time.
what.c2: It needs no kernel module and no FUSE. A single `dfs` process serves every protocol.
what.c3: File content lives in an S3-compatible bucket, with a fast [[journal]] on local disk in front of it.
what.notes: RFC 0 'Start here · In plain words': 'DittoFS is a file server that runs as an ordinary program, with no kernel module. Clients mount it over NFS or SMB, as they would mount a NAS box. Behind the protocols, file content lives in a remote object store — an S3 compatible bucket — with a fast local journal in front of it.' README.md 'What is DittoFS?' lists the protocol versions (NFSv3, v4.0, v4.1, v4.2; SMB 2 and 3) and the two binaries, dfs and dfsctl.

cast.title: The cast every deck uses
table: keeps her profile disk `ODFC_alice.vhdx`, a 30 GB file, open all day and overwrites it 64 KiB at a time, at random places
untars and compiles many small files, then removes them with `rm -rf`
cast.footer: Both connect to the same [[node]], N1. N1 keeps its [[journal]] on a local NVMe disk, and its [[remote-tier|remote tier]] is the S3 bucket `dfs-data`.
cast.notes: RFC 0 'Start here · The shared cast'. Every RFC tells its examples with this installation, so a story started in one deck continues in the next. bob has the same profile container as alice; the cluster cast (P1, P2, S1–S3, shards A and B) appears only where an RFC is about several nodes.

sees.title: What a user sees
items: Users mount a [[share]] as they would any NAS: as a drive on Windows, or as a mount point on Linux.
Their writes are answered at local-disk speed, even though the content ends up in a bucket.
A write survives a server crash once answered, and a power cut once flushed.
They see the same files over NFS and SMB, and locks hold across both protocols.
Users and permissions are the same, whichever protocol a client comes in by.
sees.notes: RFC 0 'The problem' (acknowledge small random overwrites at local-disk speed, keep every acknowledged write across a crash), 'What this RFC promises' (a write is acknowledged only once the journal can recover it), RFC 14 §7 (conflicts across protocols), RFC 19 (one ACL model). README.md 'Features' lists cross-protocol coordination and a shared cross-protocol ACL model as working today. The third bullet: RFC 1 'What this RFC promises' (an acknowledged write survives the process dying at once, and a power loss once synced, by the client's flush or within a fixed bound).

problem.title: Why not just put files in a bucket?
bucket: It is cheap, outlives any machine and is close to bottomless.
An object is written whole, so changing 64 KiB of a 30 GB file means writing a new object.
Every request takes tens of milliseconds and is billed.
It has no rename, no links, no locks and no permissions.
problem.serverTitle: What a file server must do
server: Answer small random overwrites at local-disk speed.
Keep every acknowledged write across a crash.
Honour a client's flush, whether NFS `COMMIT`, SMB `FLUSH` or `fsync`.
Offer rename, hard links, byte-range locks, deny modes and ACLs.
problem.footer: DittoFS splits the work in three. A fast [[journal]] on local disk takes every write, a bucket stores the content, and a [[metadata-store|metadata store]] records which file uses which bytes and where they are.
problem.notes: RFC 0 'Start here · The problem', both lists almost word for word, and its last paragraph for the split.

split.title: A tray, a warehouse and a ledger
split.analogy: The [[journal]] is a desk tray, the bucket a warehouse and the [[metadata-store|metadata store]] a ledger. Papers wait in the tray until the ledger says the warehouse has them, packed in boxes. Only then may the tray copy be thrown away, and a later read fetches the paper back from the warehouse.
split.stops: A box in this warehouse is never reopened to change a page, and every change goes into a new box. The ledger also notes every page that was written, even before the warehouse has it. So when a page is in neither the tray nor the warehouse, the ledger tells DittoFS whether it was never written or was written and then lost.
split.footer: The rest of this introduction follows one write through the tray, the warehouse and the ledger, under their real names.
split.notes: RFC 0 'Start here · In plain words'. The second half of 'where it stops' is the residency function (§4.2): the journal and metadata answer different questions, so their combination can name a loss instead of returning zeros. The analogy and its limit are RFC 0's own ('In plain words'). The ledger noting every write: RFC 0 'One write, followed end to end' step 2 and §4.2 (metadata records existence separately from the bytes, so a write nothing holds reads as Lost).

layers.title: Four layers, each calling the one below
table: each speaks one wire protocol, NFS or SMB
the one interface the adapters call, which decides and orders every operation
the metadata store keeps every fact about files, open state knows who holds them open or locked, and the engine moves their content
a transactional database, the local disks the journal writes to, and the bucket
layers.footer: DittoFS has one binary and one kind of node. Every [[node]] runs every layer, and when there is a single node, every call from one layer to the next is a local call.
layers.notes: RFC 0 §1.3 'The layers' table and the paragraph under it. RFC 0 calls the content part of the third layer the content subsystem: the engine (RFC 8) with the journal, carver, syncer and GC (RFCs 1–3, 9). Persistence is RFC 16 (the KV: embedded on one node, replicated in a cluster), RFC 1 (journal devices) and RFC 4 (the remote tier). Today's code has a different shape: see the slide on where today's code differs, at the end.

map.title: The component map
map.notes: RFC 0 'One write, followed end to end' (the single-node figure) and §1.3. The control plane, drawn as the management API writing records into the metadata store: RFC 0 Glossary ('the records in the metadata store that hold every setting') and RFC 23 'Start here' (the management API writes records; the node applies them). Today, architecture.md 'Core Abstraction Layers': adapters go through the Runtime, which holds the metadata service and each share's block store; dfsctl talks to the REST API served by dfs.

adapters.title: [[adapter|Adapters]] translate and decide nothing
items: One adapter serves NFSv3 and NFSv4.x, and another serves SMB 2 and 3.
They frame and decode requests, and turn each into a neutral call.
They turn the service's neutral errors into their protocol's status codes, with one table per protocol.
Permissions, locks and file operations are never decided here.
adapters.footer: The Adapters section explains them in depth.
adapters.notes: RFC 0 §1.3 (adapters: framing, compounds, replay, error codes); RFC 20 (the adapter model). The rule 'protocol handlers handle only protocol concerns' is also the first architecture invariant in CLAUDE.md for today's code. Protocol versions from README.md 'Features'. Today's code: pkg/adapter/nfs and pkg/adapter/smb, with their handlers under internal/adapter (shown nowhere on the slides; the differs slide compares behaviour, not paths).

service.title: The [[filesystem-service|filesystem service]] decides in one place
service.lead: Every call, from either adapter, passes the same steps in the same order:
steps: **Route** — when several nodes serve together as a cluster, the call goes to the file's [[primary]], the one node that decides for it. A single node routes nothing.
**Admit** — the share's state and rules must let this client in ([[admission]]).
**Authorise** — the user's [[share-grant|share grant]] is checked, then the file's own permissions.
**Open state** — the call is checked against the deny modes, locks and caching grants that others hold.
**Quota** — the space is reserved before anything changes.
**Engine** — only at the end is the content read or written.
service.notes: RFC 0 §1.3 (the filesystem service decides and orders every client operation at the primary); RFC 17 'Start here' (the six steps of every call) — the step names follow the RFC 17 deck's scene. Today's code, on the slide on where it differs: architecture.md 'Core Abstraction Layers' (adapters go through the Runtime and pkg/metadata). Route: RFC 0 'Start here · The same system as a cluster' and §1.3 (each shard has one primary; on one node it is that node).

below.title: Below the service: three parts
below.c1: It is one transactional database for every fact except the file bytes themselves: names, attributes, permissions, the [[chunk|chunks]] each file is made of, and settings.
below.c2: It records who holds each file open, locked or cached. Most of it lives in memory, on the node that is the file's [[primary]].
below.c3: It moves the file content. It drives the [[journal]], where every write lands first, the [[carver]], which packs the bytes for upload, and the [[syncer]], which uploads them to the bucket and fetches them back. It decides when each of those happens.
below.footer: Each is the subject of its own section: [[metadata-store|metadata store]], [[open-state|open state]], [[engine]], [[journal]].
below.notes: RFC 0 §1.3 (the third layer; GC belongs to the content subsystem but is the engine's sibling, run per remote namespace — RFC 8 §1, §10.5), Glossary rows for metadata store, open state and engine; RFC 14 'In plain words' ('Most of the desk lives in memory'). Today, architecture.md: metadata in BadgerDB through pkg/metadata (which also owns a lock manager per share), content in one engine.Store per share (pkg/block/engine) composing that share's journal, syncer and block store. The carver and syncer clauses: RFC 0 Glossary ('carver', 'syncer'), §5.2 (offload cuts, packs and puts).

units.title: The units, smallest to largest
table: one write as stored in the [[journal]]
a file on the journal's disk that holds many records
a run of one file's bytes, named by a keyed hash of its content
one object in the bucket, holding many chunks and written by a single put
a set of files that one node owns at a time
units.notes: RFC 0 'The shared cast · Units' and Glossary 'Units at a glance'. The namespace (a prefix in the bucket) is left out here. Today: architecture.md 'Carve: local → remote' (FastCDC min 1 MiB / avg 4 MiB / max 16 MiB, packed into 4 MiB blocks by default). The segment's size: RFC 0 Glossary 'Units at a glance' (fixed, not a setting; its value is open, RFC 28 §5 question 2; 256 MiB in the examples). Today's chunk sizes are on the differs slide.

control.title: Beside it: the [[control-plane|control plane]]
items: `dfs` is the server: it runs the adapters and serves a REST API.
[[dfsctl]] is its command-line client, for managing users, groups, shares, stores and adapters.
control.design: Every setting is a record in the [[metadata-store|metadata store]]. The [[management-api|management API]] writes records; each [[node]] reads them and makes its components match.
control.notes: README.md (the two binaries); architecture.md 'Key Interfaces' 1 and 2 (Runtime, Control Plane Store: SQLite single-node, PostgreSQL distributed) and 'Control Plane Pattern'. The design: RFC 0 Glossary 'control plane'; RFC 23 'Start here · In plain words'. RFC 23 Appendix B lists where today's code differs, e.g. API handlers call the Runtime directly after writing the database. Today's settings database and the Runtime are on the differs slide.

quizRefuse.question: In the design, build01 writes over NFS to a file alice-pc holds open over SMB with a [[deny-mode|deny mode]] against writers. Where is it refused?
options: In the NFS adapter, which looks up the file's SMB opens before passing it on.
In the SMB adapter, which holds alice-pc's open and turns other writers away.
In the filesystem service, which checks each call against the file's open state.
why: Adapters translate and decide nothing. The NFS adapter passes the write on, and later turns the service's refusal into an NFS error.
The NFS write never reaches the SMB adapter. Opens are kept in [[open-state|open state]], below the service, and no adapter decides who may write.
The [[filesystem-service|filesystem service]] runs every call through the same steps, and its open-state step finds alice-pc's deny mode and refuses the write.
quizRefuse.notes: RFC 17 'Start here' (the six steps of every call, in one order for both protocols: build01's NFSv3 write is refused at step 4 by alice's deny mode as ErrShareViolation, which the NFS adapter turns into an NFS error; if each adapter assembled the steps itself, the SMB adapter would check deny modes and the NFS adapter would not). RFC 0 §1.3 (adapters decide nothing; the filesystem service decides and orders every client operation; open state sits in the layer below it). RFC 14 §7 (conflicts across protocols). This is the design: today this state lives in each adapter plus a shared lock manager, as the slide on where today's code differs says.

write.title: One write, end to end
write.notes: RFC 0 'Start here · One write, followed end to end', steps 1–4, and §5.1, §5.2, §8.1. Step 2 simplifies: the write overwrote committed content, so the flush waits for its existence commit, which joins the next group commit; an append or hole fill is recorded within a second without the flush waiting. Step 3: chunks of about 256 KiB, each named by a keyed hash; a block of about 4 MiB; one metadata transaction records chunks and block, and only then is the journal told which extents are safe. Step 4: eviction drops only offloaded extents; disk space returns once a whole segment holds nothing still needed. Step 2's reason: RFC 0 'What this RFC promises' bullet 2 (after its stability point an overwrite never reads as the older content it replaced). Step 2's premise: until the existence commit, metadata still locates the older chunk (RFC 0 §4.2, the stale-chunk row: Lost if dropped, never the stale chunk); a lost journal device is RFC 0 §10 'Journal device lost'.

safe.title: When is a write safe?
items: A write is answered only once the [[journal]] can recover it if the DittoFS process dies.
Nothing is cut, hashed or uploaded while the client waits.
A flush, whether NFS `COMMIT`, SMB `FLUSH` or `fsync`, makes it [[durable]] across a power cut too.
The local copy is dropped only once a [[report]] confirms the bucket holds it.
A [[block]] leaves the bucket only when no file, [[snapshot|snapshot]] or [[clone]] uses it.
safe.footer: The metadata store records that each write happened within about a second. A flush waits for that only when it covers an overwrite, because until then the metadata store still points at the older bytes. A write that only extended a file or filled a hole, if lost before that, leaves the file as it was: shorter, or a hole.
safe.notes: RFC 0 'What this RFC promises' bullets 1, 3 and 4; §5.1 (content MUST NOT be chunked, hashed or transferred on the write path; existence is group-committed within existence_age, proposed 1 s, and a stability point waits for the existence commit of pending overwrites of committed content). Bullet 5 simplifies 'a block is deleted only when no file, snapshot or clone references a chunk whose record locates it there'. The fourth bullet: 'never assumed from a transfer finishing or time passing'. Bullets 1 and 3 on process death and power loss: RFC 1 'What this RFC promises' bullet 1. The footer's reason: RFC 0 'What this RFC promises' bullet 2 (an extent whose write reached its stability point never reads as older content that write replaced; if its bytes are gone the read fails) and §10 'Local content corrupt'. Clone and snapshot: RFC 0 Glossary 'Snapshots and backups'. The extend-or-hole case: RFC 0 §10 'Journal device lost' (an append or hole fill whose existence was still pending leaves no trace, and the file reads as it did before that write, shorter or a hole, not as zeros over written data).

read.title: A cold read
read.notes: RFC 0 'One write, followed end to end' step 5; the third Scenario (an overwrite during a fetch: fill never overwrites what the journal holds, the write wins); §6.1 Resolution, §6.2 Fill, §4.2 (written, no current chunk, nothing held: Lost, the read fails). Today's code keeps the same order: architecture.md 'Block Reads (verified)' — journal first, then a ranged GET of the packed block, BLAKE3-verified, hydrated back into the journal. Step 5's 'current version': RFC 0 §4.2 (an overwrite of offloaded content makes its chunk stale; dropped, it reads Lost, never the stale chunk).

partial.title: A read that is half local
partial.notes: RFC 0 §6.1 (the journal is asked first and returns the bytes it holds and the extents it does not; metadata is asked only about those), §6.2 (fill MUST NOT overwrite an extent the journal holds; it is optional). RFC 8 §7.1 (ask metadata only about what the journal does not hold), §7.2 (no byte of a chunk is copied before the whole chunk verifies; the reply is in file order, held bytes first where they are), §7.3 (filling is a decision), §7.8 (proposal: ask only the covered chunks when the missing bytes are at most a quarter of the block and the read is not sequential; otherwise the whole block). Chunks of about 256 KiB are the design's size (RFC 0); drawn not to scale. Today a cold read is a ranged GET of the packed block, BLAKE3-verified (architecture.md 'Block Reads'). Step 3 states §7.8's rule in plain words; RFC 8 marks the quarter as a fixed proposal borrowed from prior art. The four chunks are drawn starting at the read's offset; the slide places them in the middle of K1 so that §7.8's 'not sequential' condition holds, which the RFC example leaves open.

residency.title: Two sources, five answers
residency.lead: For each [[extent]], a read asks the [[journal]] first, and the [[metadata-store|metadata store]] only about what the journal does not hold. Together, their answers give the extent's [[residency]].
table: fetched from the bucket, checked, served
fails with an error, never zeros
residency.footer: The journal alone cannot tell "never written" from "written, then lost": in both cases it simply does not hold the bytes. The metadata store can, because it records that each write happened (the file's size, its holes, the ranges that were overwritten) separately from the bytes themselves. So a read returns zeros only where the metadata store records that nothing was ever written, or a hole, for example after a truncate. Residency is computed on every read and never stored.
residency.notes: RFC 0 §4.2, simplified: the RFC's table has nine rows. Left out here: a write past EOF before its existence commit (metadata says hole, journal holds it: Dirty), an overwrite of offloaded content whose chunk is now stale (Dirty while held, Lost if dropped — never the older chunk), and an offloaded all-zero extent (Absent, no fetch). Existence is group-committed within existence_age (proposal: 1 s); until then the journal is its authority (RFC 0 Glossary, 'existence'). If the journal device is lost in that window, an append or a hole fill leaves no trace and the file reads as it did before that write, shorter or a hole; an overwrite of committed content has already waited for its existence commit at its stability point, so it reads Lost (RFC 0 §10, 'Journal device lost'; §4.2). The lead: RFC 0 §6.1 (the journal is asked first; metadata only for the extents it does not hold).

quizLost.question: The [[journal]] no longer holds an extent, which metadata records as written with no current chunk. What does a read do?
options: It fails with an error, because the bytes were written and then lost.
It returns zeros, because neither source holds the bytes any more.
It fetches the chunk that held those bytes before, from the bucket.
why: Metadata shows the bytes were written, and nothing holds them now. So the extent is [[lost|Lost]], and the read fails instead of making up content.
A read returns zeros only where the [[metadata-store|metadata store]] records that nothing was written, or a hole. Here it records a write, so zeros would hide a loss.
There is no current chunk to fetch, and an older one would hand back the bytes as they were before the write, as if they were current.
quizLost.notes: RFC 0 §4.2 (residency: written, no current chunk, nothing held in the journal is Lost and the read fails; never zeros; the stale-chunk row: 'fail; never the stale chunk'), 'One write, followed end to end' step 5.

restart.title: N1 crashes in the middle of an upload
restart.notes: RFC 0 §1.4 (put intents: abandoned at start, before the first offload) and 'Scenarios · N1 crashes in the middle of an upload', steps 1–6, and §10 'Crash'. A block name is minted afresh for each put attempt and never reused (RFC 8); the orphan object is collected by GC (RFC 9 §5). The NFS write verifier changes on every restart, so NFS clients resend unstable writes (RFC 0 §1.4). Outcome, in the RFC's words: the failed upload costs time and bucket space, never data. The put intent is a metadata record (RFC 0 Glossary 'Metadata records'); a single node abandons every intent at start because it is the only writer, so every attempt an earlier process began has ended (RFC 0 §1.4); I9: a block name is minted by one put attempt and put by no other.

survive.title: What a restart keeps
survive.c1: If only the DittoFS process died, every write the [[journal]] answered is kept, because the operating system still has it. A power cut also loses what the system had not yet written to disk, so only writes already [[sync|synced]] are kept. The journal syncs at every flush, and on its own within about a second. Metadata and the bucket's content are kept too.
survive.c2: The journal rebuilds its index from its own files. An upload that was cut short is done again, because its bytes are still [[dirty|Dirty]].
survive.c3: Most [[open-state|open state]] is held in memory and is lost. Clients take back their opens and locks during a [[grace-period|grace period]] after the restart.
survive.footer: An [[smb-durable-open|SMB-durable open]] does not survive a restart. A [[persistent-open|persistent open]] does, because it is written to the metadata store.
survive.notes: RFC 1 'What the RFC promises' (an acknowledged write survives the process dying at once, and a host crash once synced — by the client's flush or within a fixed bound, 1 s proposed); RFC 0 §10 'Crash'; RFC 14 §8 (what is durable: opens and locks volatile and reclaimed in grace, caching grants never reclaimed) and §8.1. Connections and sessions are lost too; clients reconnect. Process death versus power loss: RFC 1 'Scenarios · The power fails half a second after a write nobody flushed' (had only the process died the operating system would still hold the record; an unsynced record does not survive host loss) and §5.2 (the sync timer, 1 s proposed).

outage.title: The bucket stops answering
steps: alice-pc keeps writing. The [[journal]] stores each write on local disk and answers her as usual.
No upload succeeds, so nothing written since the bucket stopped can be [[evict|evicted]] from the journal.
A read of content whose only copy is in the bucket fails with an error. It never returns zeros.

If the journal fills up, new writes wait. NFS clients are answered [[retry-later]] and try again. SMB holds each request pending, and answers disk full only if it is still waiting at its pending timeout. No answered write is dropped.
When the bucket answers again, offload uploads the backlog on its own, with no operator step.
outage.footer: While uploads keep failing, the share reports a health condition, not just a line in a log.
outage.notes: RFC 0 'Scenarios · The bucket stops answering for an afternoon', steps 1–6, and §10 'Remote tier unavailable', 'Journal at capacity, remote unavailable'. NFS clients retry; SMB holds the request pending up to adapters.smb.pending_timeout, and only there answers STATUS_DISK_FULL (§10 'Journal at capacity, remote available', §10.3). Outcome: no acknowledged write is dropped to make room; clients wait instead.

failures.title: Every failure has one behaviour
table: writes still go into the journal, but reads of content that is only in the bucket fail
writes are answered with [[retry-later]] while offload uploads the bytes, eviction drops their local copies and [[repack]] gives the disk space back
writes are still staged in the journal, but after 30 s with no metadata commit they are answered [[retry-later]] until a commit succeeds, while reads go on
the journal rebuilds its index, and unfinished work resumes
content already in the bucket is safe, but the shares that journal served wait for an operator
failures.footer: Every condition clears on its own once its cause is gone, except three that wait for an operator: a lost journal disk, a lost metadata store, and a node started from a copied or restored disk image, because the copy and the original could both serve and answer clients as one server.
failures.notes: RFC 0 §10, simplified, and §10.2. The full row is 'Journal at capacity, remote available'; repack is RFC 1 §7.2. The 30 s row is the self-fence (§1.4; §10 'Metadata store stalled or erroring': writes and stability points answer retry-later, reads continue, and the node resumes when a write commits). A lost journal device: after the operator's acknowledgement, content never offloaded whose existence was committed reads as Lost. The three exceptions (§10.2, 'What this RFC promises'): a lost journal device on a share no other journal holds, a lost metadata store (an operator starts a recovery import from the newest catalog backup), and a node started from a copied or restored image. Why a copied image waits: RFC 0 §10.2, the decision on a node started from a copied image (two copies that both resume would answer clients as one server). Repack is what returns journal space (RFC 0 §8.2; evict alone frees none, §8.1). The footer's first exception is stated for one node: on a single node no other journal holds a share's content; in a cluster a replica's journal can take the shard over with no operator (§10 'Journal device lost').

quizFull.question: The bucket has been down for hours and N1's [[journal]] is full. What happens to build01's next NFS write?
options: N1 evicts older writes that are not in the bucket yet, to make room for it.
N1 answers retry-later, and build01 keeps resending it until space frees up.
N1 refuses it with a disk-full error, and build01's compile job stops.
why: The journal may [[evict]] only bytes the bucket already holds. Writes made since the bucket stopped have no other copy, so evicting them would lose answered writes.
Space will come back once uploads resume, so N1 answers [[retry-later|retry-later]]. NFS clients wait and retry for as long as the outage lasts, and no answered write is lost.
A full journal gets its space back once uploads resume. So N1 answers retry-later rather than disk full, and build01 waits instead of failing.
quizFull.notes: RFC 0 'Scenarios · The bucket stops answering for an afternoon' step 5; §10 'Journal at capacity, remote unavailable' (refuse the write with retry-later, since space is coming from repack and from offload once the remote returns; the client retries for as long as the outage lasts; I2 forbids evicting a Dirty extent, so refusal is the only behaviour that does not lose data; no space is answered only for a cause that needs an operator, or to an SMB request held past its pending cap, which is why the question uses build01's NFS write).

twoproto.title: Two protocols, one file
twoproto.lead: Every request for a file, over NFS or SMB, is checked against one table of [[open-state|open state]], kept on the file's [[primary]].
items: alice-pc opens a file over SMB with a [[deny-mode|deny mode]] that keeps writers out, so build01's NFS write to it is refused.
An SMB [[byte-range-lock|lock]] is mandatory, so it refuses the NFS reads and writes it forbids across its range.
An NFS lock is advisory, so it refuses only other locks, never reads or writes.
A [[caching-grant|caching grant]] that conflicts with a request is [[recall|recalled]] before the request goes ahead.
twoproto.notes: RFC 14 'In plain words', 'A scenario: an NFS build tool and an SMB editor share one file' and §7 'Conflicts across protocols'. A caching grant is an SMB lease or oplock, or an NFSv4 delegation; it is recalled in the holder's own protocol, whatever protocol caused the conflict. Today: RFC 14 Appendix B (NFSv4 state in the NFS adapter, SMB leases in the SMB lease manager, locks in pkg/metadata/lock); README.md lists bidirectional lease/delegation breaks between SMB and NFS as working. Today's split is on the differs slide.

identity.title: Who you are, checked in one place
items: The adapter passes on who the client claims to be, and what, if anything, proved it.

[[admission|Admission]] applies the share's rules. They say which security flavours and which clients it accepts, and which users are squashed, so that root, for example, acts as the share's anonymous user.
The user's [[share-grant|share grant]] sets a ceiling, and within it the file's mode or ACL decides.
File permissions are decided in a single [[chokepoint]], with one ACL model for NFS and SMB alike.
identity.notes: RFC 17 (admission, authorisation, the chokepoint), RFC 18 (identity and squashing), RFC 19 (one ACL model, the share ceiling). AUTH_SYS only claims an identity; Kerberos and NTLM prove one — the neutral Identity records which. Today: CLAUDE.md architecture invariant 2 (every operation carries a *metadata.AuthContext; Runtime.ApplyIdentityMapping squashes in one place for both adapters; permission checks belong in pkg/metadata). Squashing: RFC 18 'Start here · In plain words' ('squash: replacing the caller's principal with the share's anonymous one') and its root-squash example. Today's code in plain words, as the differs slide puts it: the description of the caller is metadata.AuthContext, the shared squashing function is Runtime.ApplyIdentityMapping, and the metadata layer is pkg/metadata.

cluster.title: Later: more than one node
items: The first release runs on one [[node]], with an embedded metadata store and no replicas.
A cluster runs several identical nodes that share one replicated metadata store and one bucket.
Each [[shard]], which is one [[share]] by default, has one [[primary]] node that decides every call on its files.
A call that arrives at another node is forwarded to the primary by that node's [[gateway-node|gateway]], which decides nothing itself.
Each node's journals are replicated to other nodes, so a replica can take over the shards of a node that is lost.
cluster.footer: The cluster comes after the first release.
cluster.notes: RFC 0 'Start here · The same system as a cluster', §1.3 ('Each shard has one primary'), §1.4 (the single-node profile; RFC 10, 11 and 15 carry the status deferred), §10 'Node lost' (cluster). Today, architecture.md 'Multi-Node Metadata': Badger serves exactly one dfs process. RFCs 10, 11 and 15 describe the cluster.

differs.title: Where today's code differs from the design
table: one per share, in its own directory
one per disk, shared by the shares on it
1–16 MiB, and a chunk that two files share is stored once, by [[deduplication]]
about 256 KiB, and in the first release each file's chunks are uploaded even when identical
the [[runtime|Runtime]], which squashes identities, and `pkg/metadata`, which checks permissions
opens and caching grants in each adapter, locks in one shared lock manager
one table per file, at its [[primary]]
a control-plane database, SQLite or PostgreSQL
records in the [[metadata-store|metadata store]], applied by each [[node]]
differs.footer: With deduplication, offload skips a chunk it is told is already stored, and its local copy can then be dropped. One wrong answer would leave those bytes stored nowhere, so the design leaves deduplication out of the first release. The section decks explain the design, and `docs/internals/architecture.md` describes the code as it is.
differs.notes: Today: architecture.md 'Per-Share Block Store Isolation' and 'Block Store — Local Journal Tier' (one journal directory per share), 'Carve' (FastCDC 1/4/16 MiB, dedup against the SyncedHashStore), 'Key Interfaces'; RFC 14 and RFC 23 Appendix B. Design: RFC 0 §1 and RFC 1 (one journal per device), Glossary 'chunk' and §3.1 (the first release does not deduplicate across files), §1.3, RFC 14 §3, RFC 0 Glossary 'control plane'. The footer's reason: RFC 0 §3.1, the decision that cross-file deduplication is off in the first release (its oracle is the one component where a single wrong answer, a chunk reported stored that is stored nowhere, loses data). The chain: with deduplication, offload references an already-stored chunk instead of uploading it, and the extent is then reported offloaded and becomes evictable; RFC 8 §6.5 names a chunk reported stored that is stored nowhere as the one wrong answer that loses data. Rows 3–5, today: architecture.md 'Core Abstraction Layers' and 'Key Interfaces' 1 and 2 (Runtime; Control Plane Store, SQLite single-node or PostgreSQL distributed); CLAUDE.md architecture invariant 2 (Runtime.ApplyIdentityMapping squashes for both adapters; permission checks in pkg/metadata); RFC 14 Appendix B (NFSv4 state in the NFS adapter, SMB leases in the SMB lease manager, byte-range locks in pkg/metadata/lock); RFC 23 Appendix B (API handlers call the Runtime after writing the database). Design: RFC 17 'Start here' (admit and authorise in the service), RFC 23 'Start here' (each node reads the records and applies them). The Settings row leaves out that today the REST API writes the database and then calls the Runtime (RFC 23 Appendix B).

steps: Each client talks to the [[adapter]] for its protocol, and both adapters call the same [[filesystem-service|filesystem service]].
The service checks [[open-state|open state]] for who holds the file open, and asks the [[metadata-store|metadata store]] for names and permissions.
The file's bytes go to the [[engine]], which writes them to the [[journal]] on local disk. Later, in the background, they go on to the [[remote-tier|remote tier]], the bucket.
Off to the side, [[dfsctl]] calls the [[management-api|management API]], which stores every setting as a record in the metadata store.
At 09:00 alice-pc writes 64 KiB to her profile disk. N1 appends one [[record]] to the [[journal]] on its local disk and answers her. Nothing is cut, hashed or uploaded while she waits.

Right after, alice-pc sends a flush, and the journal [[sync|syncs]] the record to its disk. Until now, the metadata store points at the older version of these 64 KiB. So the flush also waits until it records that her write happened, its [[existence]]. From then on, if the journal's disk were lost before the upload, a read would fail with an error instead of returning the older bytes.

At 09:04, in the background, N1 [[offload|offloads]] the bytes. It cuts them into [[chunk|chunks]], packs them into a [[block]] and puts the block to `dfs-data`. Once the bucket has stored it, the metadata store records chunks and block, and only then is the journal told the bytes are safe.
At 18:00 the journal is filling up. It [[evict|evicts]] its local copy of those 64 KiB, which it may do because the bucket now holds them.
The next morning alice-pc reads those 64 KiB again. N1 asks the [[journal]] first, and the journal no longer holds them.
N1 then asks the [[metadata-store|metadata store]], which answers that the bytes are in chunk C, inside block K1 in the bucket.
N1 gets those bytes from `dfs-data`, checks them against their hash and sends them to alice-pc.
N1 may also keep a local copy of them, which is called a [[fill]]. A fill never overwrites a newer write that the journal holds.

Suppose instead the metadata store had said these bytes were written again after their last upload, so no chunk in the bucket holds their current version. With nothing in the journal either, they are [[lost|Lost]], and the read fails with an error rather than returning zeros or the older version.
N1 starts an [[offload]]. It first records in the metadata store a [[put-intent|put intent]], a note naming the new block, K7, and then starts the upload to the bucket.
N1 crashes before the metadata store has recorded K7. So the bytes it was uploading stay [[dirty|Dirty]] in the journal, not yet offloaded.
When N1 restarts, the [[journal]] rebuilds its index from its own files. A last record that was only half written counts as never written.

Before it serves clients again, the [[engine]] records in the metadata store the [[existence]] of the writes it had not recorded yet. It also abandons the intent for K7, since no upload begun before the crash can still be running.

Later, [[gc|GC]] deletes whatever K7 left in the bucket. A new offload uploads the same bytes under a new name, K8, because every upload attempt gets a fresh [[block-name|block name]] that is never reused.

partial.dropped: C1's first 64 KiB: old version, discarded
steps: alice-pc has just rewritten 64 KiB of a file, starting at 2 GiB, and now reads 1 MiB from that same point. N1 asks the [[journal]] first: it still holds the 64 KiB just written, and lists the other 960 KiB as [[missing]], not held on this disk.
Only for those 960 KiB does N1 ask the [[metadata-store|metadata store]] where they are: in four [[chunk|chunks]] in the middle of [[block]] K1, whose only copy is in the bucket.

N1 fetches a whole block when a read needs more than a quarter of it, starts at the block's beginning, or picks up where the previous read ended. This read needs 960 KiB of block K1, about 4 MiB, and starts in its middle, so N1 downloads from `dfs-data` only the four chunks it covers.

Before using a single byte of a chunk, N1 checks the whole chunk against its hash. C1 also holds the first 64 KiB as they were before alice-pc's rewrite: N1 throws those away, because the newer version is in the journal.

N1 sends the reply in file order: the 64 KiB from the journal, then the 960 KiB from the chunks. It may also keep the downloaded bytes on its disk with a [[fill]], so the next read finds them there; but a fill never writes over the 64 KiB the journal holds.
